summary: Baptism (Greek baptisma, from baptizein, to dip or immerse) is the Christian rite of initiation, the water rite by which a person is incorporated into the Church and, in most traditions, cleansed of sin and reborn. Its warrant is the New Testament: the risen Christ's command to baptize all nations 'in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost' (Matthew 28:19), Peter's Pentecost call to 'be baptized ... for the remission of sins' (Acts 2:38), Paul's teaching that the baptized are 'baptized into his death' and raised to 'walk in newness of life' (Romans 6:3-4), and the saying that one must be 'born of water and of the Spirit' (John 3:5); it is described in the earliest church order, the Didache. The traditions differ over who is baptized (infants or professing believers), how (immersion or pouring), and what the rite effects (sacramental regeneration or the symbolic seal of a faith already held), and those differing accounts are recorded here as the attributed teachings of each tradition.
description:
Baptism is the rite of Christian initiation: a washing with water, administered in the threefold name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, by which a person is made a member of the Church. Across the traditions it is understood as the sacrament (or, for some, the ordinance) that marks entry into the Christian community and, in most accounts, effects or seals the forgiveness of sins, union with the death and resurrection of Christ, and rebirth by the Holy Spirit.

Its scriptural basis is drawn chiefly from the New Testament. The Gospel of Matthew closes with the risen Christ's charge, read across the traditions as the Great Commission and the institution of the rite: 'Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost' (Matthew 28:19). At Pentecost, Peter answers the crowd, 'Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost' (Acts 2:38). Paul reads baptism as incorporation into Christ's own death and resurrection: 'so many of us as were baptized into Jesus Christ were baptized into his death', so that 'we are buried with him by baptism into death', and as Christ was raised 'even so we also should walk in newness of life' (Romans 6:3-4). The Johannine saying that 'Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God' (John 3:5) is read across much of the tradition as pointing to baptismal regeneration. Alongside these stands the baptism of John and the baptism of Jesus in the Jordan, and the frequent New Testament association of baptism with the forgiveness of sins and the gift of the Spirit.

The practice is attested very early. The Didache (chapter 7), an early church order, directs: 'baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit' in 'running water' (living water); where running water is not available, other water may be used, and 'if you have no cold water, in warm'; and where neither is possible, 'pour water on the head three times in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit', with fasting beforehand by the one baptizing, the one baptized, and any others who can. This early text already shows both the fixed trinitarian formula and a flexibility of mode (immersion preferred, pouring permitted).

The later traditions share the rite while differing over its subjects, its mode, and its effect, and these positions are recorded here as attributed teachings, not adjudicated. On the question of subjects, the Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed, and Anglican traditions practise the baptism of infants, understanding the child to be received into the covenant community and cleansed of original sin, while the Baptist and Anabaptist traditions restrict baptism to those who can profess faith for themselves (believer's baptism, credobaptism), holding that baptism presupposes a personal confession. On the question of mode, some traditions baptize by full immersion (the ordinary Orthodox practice and the characteristic Baptist practice), others by affusion (pouring) or aspersion (sprinkling), and the Didache already shows the range. On the question of effect, the Catholic, Orthodox, and Lutheran traditions teach baptismal regeneration, that the sacrament truly conveys the grace it signifies (the remission of sins and rebirth by the Spirit), an account associated with the reading of John 3:5 and Titus 3:5; the Reformed tradition treats baptism as a sign and seal of the covenant of grace; and the Baptist and much of the Anabaptist tradition understand baptism as an ordinance, an obedient symbol and public profession of a regeneration and faith already received, rather than a means by which grace is conferred. Sociologically, across all these accounts baptism functions as the rite of entry into the religious community, the threshold act by which an outsider becomes a member of the Church, comparable in that social role to entry rites in other traditions. This entry describes the rite and its shared scriptural and early institution, and reports the divergent accounts of its subjects, mode, and effect as the attributed positions of their respective traditions.
editorial_notes:
This entry describes baptism and reports the disputed questions of its subjects (infant baptism in the Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed, and Anglican traditions versus believer's baptism in the Baptist and Anabaptist traditions), its mode (immersion, affusion, aspersion), and its effect (sacramental regeneration in the Catholic, Orthodox, and Lutheran accounts; sign and seal of the covenant in the Reformed account; ordinance and symbolic profession in the Baptist and Anabaptist accounts) strictly as the attributed teachings of each tradition, per neutrality principles #1, #2, and #4. The editor does not adjudicate which account is correct; the infant-versus-believer and sacramental-versus-symbolic disputes are handled by attribution throughout, and neither is presented as the biblical or original position.

Sourcing triangulates the three lenses per neutrality #8 as adapted for Christianity. (a) Academic historian of doctrine and liturgy: Everett Ferguson, Baptism in the Early Church (Eerdmans, 2009), the standard scholarly history of baptismal thought, practice, and liturgy in the first five centuries. (b) The primary corpus, read directly and open: Matthew 28:18-20, Acts 2:38, Romans 6:3-4, and John 3:5 (biblehub, KJV), and the Didache 7 (CCEL, Richardson) for the earliest baptismal instruction. (c) A contemporary Christian theologian on-topic: Alister E. McGrath, Christian Theology: An Introduction (Wiley-Blackwell), the chapter on the sacraments, which lays out the range of positions on baptism. No encyclopedias, no Wikipedia, no tertiary sources.

Relation targets present in the dataset: sacraments. The compares_with targets shahada (Islam) and giyur (Judaism) exist in the dataset. Each compares_with note states the shared question (how a person enters the religious community) and the difference, and ranks nothing, per neutrality #10.

relations.note: Baptism is one of the sacraments (one of the seven in the Catholic and Orthodox reckoning, one of the two commonly retained in the Reformation traditions, and, for the Baptist and much of the Anabaptist tradition, an ordinance rather than a sacrament); situated within the tradition's sacramental theology.

Shared question: how a person formally enters the religious community. Difference: baptism is a water rite administered by the Church that, in most Christian accounts, effects or seals incorporation into the body of Christ and (in the sacramental accounts) the remission of sin, whereas the shahada is a verbal profession of faith, the spoken testimony by which a person becomes a Muslim. The comparison states the shared social function (a threshold act of entry) and the difference; it ranks nothing and equates nothing. Target (shahada) exists in the dataset.

Shared question: how a person from outside joins the religious community. Difference: Christian baptism is a single water rite of initiation open to all who come to the faith, whereas giyur (conversion to Judaism) is a halakhic process, in the traditional account involving acceptance of the commandments, circumcision for males, and immersion in a mikveh before a rabbinic court, joining a people as well as a faith. The comparison states the shared question of entry and the difference; it ranks nothing and equates nothing. Target (giyur) exists in the dataset.

historical_period.note: The rite is traced to the New Testament: the baptism of Jesus, the risen Christ's command in Matthew 28:19, and the apostolic practice reported in Acts (conventionally from c. 30); attested in the earliest post-apostolic church order, the Didache (chapter 7). No end date is asserted; baptism is continuous in Christian practice to the present. The distinctive later disputes over infant versus believer's baptism sharpened at the Reformation (the sixteenth-century Anabaptist movement), and the disputes over the mode and the effect of the rite run through the whole tradition.

sources.citation: The Holy Bible, Matthew 28:18-20 (KJV): the risen Christ's charge, 'Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost: Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you', preceded by 'All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth' and followed by 'I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world.' Read across the traditions as the Great Commission and the dominical institution of baptism; the primary-corpus lens for the command and the trinitarian formula.

sources.citation: The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), chapter 7 (Concerning Baptism), Richardson translation. 'Baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit' in 'running water' (living water); if running water is unavailable, in other water, and 'if you have no cold water, in warm'; failing both, 'pour water on the head three times in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit'; with fasting beforehand by the baptizer, the baptized, and any others who can. Early church order; the primary-corpus lens for the earliest baptismal instruction, showing the fixed trinitarian formula and the flexibility of mode.

sources.citation: Ferguson, Everett. Baptism in the Early Church: History, Theology, and Liturgy in the First Five Centuries. Grand Rapids, MI: William B. Eerdmans, 2009. The standard scholarly history of baptismal thought, practice, and liturgy across the first five centuries, arranged by century and region, covering the literary, epigraphic, and material evidence and the meanings attributed to baptism (chiefly the forgiveness of sins and the gift of the Holy Spirit). The academic-historian lens.
